subject: human brain
title: What If You Could Never Make a New Memory? One Man Lived 55 Years Like That

scenes.text: What if you could never make another memory? One man lived that way for 55 years.
In 1953, a surgeon tried to cure a 27-year-old's severe epilepsy by removing a small part of his brain, including much of the hippocampus.
Afterwards, he could no longer form new memories. Whatever happened to him slipped away.
Scientists studied him for decades under the initials H.M. They had to introduce themselves every time they met.
Yet he could still get better at new physical skills with practice. So the brain doesn't keep all its memories in one place.
He died in 2008. His brain was cut into 2,401 slices, and the 53 hours of slicing were streamed live. The man who couldn't remember became one of the most famous brains in science.

description:
What if you lost the ability to store new memories? It happened to a man known to science as patient H.M.
In 1953, aged 27, he had part of his medial temporal lobe, including much of the hippocampus, removed to treat severe epilepsy. From then on he could not form new memories, although he could still improve at motor skills with practice. His case gave the first conclusive evidence that the hippocampus is fundamental for memory. After his death in 2008 his brain was cut into 2,401 slices in a 53-hour procedure shown live online.

first_comment: The 2014 study of his brain found the surgeon had removed less than everyone thought. Which memory would you least want to lose, and what should we run through next?
